chapter_theme: The Sadasiva linga: Sadasiva, five-faced, fifteen-eyed and ten-armed, is the form shared by the gods, bindu, nada and Shakti; through Shakti the directions, Vedas, religions and tattvas unfold. His faces and limb-mantras are set on the body, the poet takes him into his heart, and the chapter ends with one's own body as the linga and the linga as the syllable Om.
structure_note: Sadasiva's form and what he holds in common (1730, 1731); the unfolding through Shakti, in a chain where each verse takes up the last one's closing word (1732 to 1734); the five faces, their colours and the Lord in the heart (1735, 1736); Shakti and Siva as all the tattvas (1737, 1738); devotion (1739, 1740); the faces and limb-mantras set on the body and the shapes of Shakti (1741 to 1745); the Lord in the body and heart (1746 to 1750); Om and the linga (1751, 1752).

1730.reading: Sadasiva, a pearl of good light, stands with his two feet together on the pedestal, with arms spreading two and eight, five faces to be sought, and three fives more.
1730.nuance: A meditation image. The two and eight arms make ten, as 1736 says; செங்கையின் மூவைந்து (three fives with the red hands) is unclear, but 1736 gives fifteen eyes, so the fifteen are probably his eyes.

1731.reading: Brahma, tall Vishnu, Rudra, Maheshvara above them and the five-faced one above him, bindu and nada, and the supporting Shakti with Siva: Sadasiva is what is common to them all.
1731.nuance: The list follows the traditional ascending order of the deities who govern the levels of the cosmos. சாதாரணம் (common) may mean Sadasiva is shared by all of them, or is the general form that includes them.

1732.reading: Within the Shakti that comes to be, the kalas take their place and the rays rise; once he is seated within her, the ten directions are within that Shakti.
1732.nuance: ஆகின்ற சத்தி opens every line. கலை may be the kalas of cosmology, and கதிர் the rays of sun and moon. Who is seated (அமர்ந்த) is not said; Sadasiva is the natural subject.

1733.reading: Within those directions are settled the six limbs of the Veda, the four Vedas, the path of chariyai, and the religious systems.
1733.nuance: The verse takes up 1732's last words (அத்திசை) and hands its own last word (சமயம்) to 1734. Placing the Vedas, chariyai and the religions within Shakti's directions makes them all products of her unfolding.

1734.reading: From that religious order arise the ten states, the twelve signs of the zodiac and the forty-eight bodies, and from it arises Sadasiva himself.
1734.nuance: சமயம் may here mean religious system, as in 1733, or appointed time and order. அவத்தை ஈரைந்து (ten states of the soul) and சரீரம் ஆறெட்டு (six eights of bodies) are technical and I can't fix them.

1735.reading: The five faces he gave me, his servant, face the zenith, east, south, north and west, and are coloured crystal, saffron, dark collyrium, red and milk-white.
1735.nuance: The faces are traditionally Isana, Tatpurusha, Aghora, Vamadeva and Sadyojata, matched in order with the colours. அடியேற்கு அருளிய (granted to me, the servant) turns an iconographic list into a vision given in grace.

1736.reading: He has five faces, fifteen eyes, ten hands and ten weapons, and this Lord has entered my heart and stands filling it.
1736.nuance: The play on அஞ்சு (five) fills three lines and gives way in the fourth to நெஞ்சு (heart), so the counted form ends inside the devotee.

1737.reading: Shakti and Sadasiva are the earth and the cosmos; Shakti and Siva fill all that is fixed and all that moves; Shakti and Sadasiva are form and the formless; Shakti and Siva are the thirty-six tattvas.
1737.nuance: Each line opens with சத்தி and pairs her with Siva or Sadasiva, so the verse never names one without the other.

1738.reading: The tattvas are the formless and all that moves and does not move, they are form and the rising of joy; all tattvas stand as everything, and Sadasiva is the tattva itself.
1738.nuance: தத்துவம் opens every line, taking up 1737's last word. சுகோதயம் (the rising of joy) is unclear here; it may name a state or the pleasures the tattvas give.

1739.reading: Declare that Sadasiva, welling up within, is our Lord: describe him in other words and he stands beyond them; apart from the gods whose work is lofty speech, he has entered my mind.
1739.nuance: மிகைப்பொருள் (surplus meaning) suggests he exceeds any other description. Line 3 (ஏறுரை செய்தொழில் வானவர்) is unclear: it may be the gods who make proud claims, or ஏறு may be Siva's bull. மாறுசெய்வான் may mean he opposes or he differs from them.

1740.reading: Clear in understanding, I have held steady within me the first Lord whose mind is full of grace, with his dark throat, raised axe and bright crescent in his curling red hair.
1740.nuance: The dark throat (from the poison he drank), the axe and the crescent are Siva's usual marks. The verse moves from seeing the form to holding it within (தெளிந்திருந்தேனே), which is meditation.

1741.reading: Telling the five faces in which Shakti stands, the verse places Vamadeva as the highest, Tatpurusha in the east as the head, and Aghora and Isana after them.
1741.nuance: The verse is hard to divide. காற்றிடில் may be for கூற்றிடில் (if one tells); உரையத்து, தத்துவம் பூருவம் and அத்தரு கோரம் மருடத்து do not divide clearly. The five faces are also the five Brahma mantras of Agamic worship.

1742.reading: Isana is the crown of the head, Tatpurusha the face, Aghora the heart, Vamadeva the secret parts, and Shakti the feet.
1742.nuance: This is the placing (nyasa) of the five faces on the worshipper's body. The feet traditionally belong to Sadyojata, so சத்தி here may name that face or the power in it. தாணுவின் தன்முகம் (Sthanu's own face) is read as the face.

1743.reading: Heart, head, tuft, long armour and eye are the limbs; the flawless bindu is green, the crest flashes like lightning, and the ten weapons are like a red flame.
1743.nuance: நெஞ்சு, சிரம், சிகை, கவசம், கண் are the limb-mantras (anga mantras) of Agamic worship, with the weapon (astra) completing them. The colours belong to the tradition of meditation on them; சேகரி may mean the crest or a name of Shakti.

1744.reading: The heart is the Lord's power of knowledge, the head the supreme Shakti, the tuft and the armour his power of will, and his power of action is in the supreme eye.
1744.nuance: The limbs of 1743 are matched with the Lord's powers of knowledge, will and action (ஞான, இச்சை, கிரியை). How சிகையாதி and வண்ணம் divide between tuft and armour is unclear.

1745.reading: Shakti stands moving in the square, rests in the hexagon, and stays moving in the circle; Sadasiva is Shakti's form.
1745.nuance: சலம் may be water or movement. The square, hexagon and circle may be the shapes of a linga's pedestal or the diagrams of worship. சயனம் (lying, bed) is unclear here.

1746.reading: However long one calls on Nandi who bears the deer, he stands in the five as a single flame; rising past the navel to the lotus, Nandi stands above, in the nine.
1746.nuance: நந்தி ends a word in every line. மான் நந்தி may be Siva holding the deer or 'great Nandi'. The five, the navel, the lotus and the nine are yogic places in the body, but which ones is not fixed; கால் நந்தி may be the breath.

1747.reading: Our Lord stays joined with the body and always moves within it; when it rose to the head and was set right, I stood and worshipped Siva's feet within my heart.
1747.nuance: What rises to the head (தென்தலைக்கு ஏற) is unstated; tradition takes it as the breath or kundalini. தென்தலை may be 'the fair head' or a corruption. The worship is inner: the feet are found in the heart.

1748.reading: I came to know the bright reality in the world, brought him in and made my heart his temple on earth; I have joined the Pure One, and this is truth, not falsehood; I bowed, and the sun's song is the sound.
1748.nuance: The verbs run in sequence: knew, brought, joined, bowed. குவலயம் கோயில் என் நெஞ்சம் can mean my heart is a temple on earth, or the earth and my heart are both his temple. The last phrase, பகலவன் பாட்டும் ஒலியே, is obscure.

1749.reading: When fierce fire blazes through those three, the fourteen bear it, and in their midst rise the beginning and the end; these here become one's body and the moon.
1749.nuance: The three may be the sun, moon and fire, or three nadis, and ஈரேழு (fourteen) may be the worlds or the body's regions. இந்து (moon) is traditionally the cooling nectar at the head. I can't fix the sense with any confidence.

1750.reading: One's own body stands as one's Sivalinga, one's body stands as Sadasiva, one's body is one's own Siva and Siva-bliss, and one's body becomes the Supreme itself.
1750.nuance: தன்மேனி (one's own body) opens every line, and தற்- (one's own) is prefixed to linga, Siva and bliss. The verse draws the chapter from Sadasiva's form to the worshipper's own body.

1751.reading: No one knows that he is the letter A and that she, the Lady spread through the world, is U; the two together become the whole earth and rise, transformed, as sound.
1751.nuance: தாரம் may mean consort, so the two are Siva and Shakti, or the sacred syllable (tara, Om), of which A and U are parts. Sengalvaraya compares the first line with Kural 1.

1752.reading: In the linga, Om is the good pedestal, M fills its neck, U fills its inner circle, and A is the linga itself, filled with bindu and nada.
1752.nuance: The syllable Om is mapped onto the parts of the linga: pedestal, neck (கண்டம்), inner circle and shaft, with bindu and nada, the dot and resonance of Om, in the shaft. இலிங்கம் opens every line.

links.note: 1726 says the human body's form is the Sivalinga, Sadasiva and the dance; 1750 says it of one's own body (தன்மேனி) and goes on to Siva-bliss and the Supreme itself.

Both start from the letter A. The Kural compares: as A comes first among letters, the Primal Lord comes first for the world; Tirumular makes the Lord himself the letter A, with Shakti as U, and the two become the earth and sound. The simile becomes an identity.
Both analyse Om into A, U and M with bindu and nada. 1926 places them in the ascent of the kalas; 1752 maps them onto the parts of the linga.

1730 gives Sadasiva's meditation form with five faces (முகம்ஐந்து), ten arms and fifteen eyes. 1569 says the Lord has five faces and also a sixth, turned downward (அதோமுகம்). Set together, 1569 adds to the five-faced form of 1730 a hidden sixth face that the meditation image leaves out.

1731 runs up the ladder Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Maheshvara, the five-faced one, bindu, nada and Shakti, and calls Sadasiva what is common to all (சாதாரணமாம்). 400 has Sadasiva and the others, Isa, Hara, Mal and Brahma, go out together within unfailing Shakti (போகாத சத்தியுட் போந்துடன்). Both treat the graded gods as one series held within Shakti and Sadasiva.

1733 places the six limbs, the four Vedas, chariyai and the religious systems (சமயம்) within the directions of Shakti. Song 575 defines Sivayoga as seeing the five elements, the six religions (ஆறு சமயமும்), mantras, Vedas, Puranas and letters abiding as one form (ஏக வடிவம்). Both gather the Vedas and the rival faiths into a single source rather than ranking them.

1735 gives the five faces as the zenith and the four quarters, each with a colour, and says they were granted to the poet (அடியேற்கு அருளிய முகம்). 1742 places the same five faces on the worshipper's body: Isana at the crown, Tatpurusha the face, Aghora the heart, Vamadeva the secret parts, Shakti the feet. Together they carry the five faces from the directions of space onto the body.

1736 counts Sadasiva's form, five faces, fifteen eyes, ten hands and ten weapons, and ends with him entering and filling the heart (நெஞ்சு புகுந்து நிறைந்துநின்றானே). Song 568 asks to hold in thought every day (நாளு நினைவது) Murugan's flower faces, twelve arms, two feet, consorts, vel and peacock. Both are meditation by counting the god's form limb by limb, one on Siva, one on Murugan, and both end the list in the devotee's mind.

1739 says that if one describes Sadasiva in other words he stands beyond them as surplus meaning (மிகைப்பொருளாய் நிற்கும்). Song 1175 names a reality that debaters cannot speak (வாதிகள் பாஷிக்கத் தகாது) and that no reason can state (ஏதுச்செப் பொணாதது). Both hold that speech falls short of the Lord; 1739 still keeps one sentence, that he is our Lord, while 1175 works only through negatives.

1742 places the five faces, which are also the five Brahma mantras, on the worshipper's body, from Isana at the crown to Shakti at the feet. Song 1165 lays the letters of நமசிவய on the Lord's form, na the feet, ma the belly, si the chest, va the mouth, ya the crown (நகரமிரு பாதமாகி ... வாய் வகரமாகி). Both map sacred sounds onto a body, head to foot; 1742 onto the worshipper's, 1165 onto the god's.

1744 matches the limbs of worship to the Lord's powers: the heart his power of knowledge (ஞான சத்தி), the tuft and armour his will (இச்சை), and action (கிரியை) in the eye. 2459 makes Shakti the body of the Supreme, taking on the distinctions of will, knowledge and the rest (இச்சையில் ஞானாதி பேதமாய்). 1744 applies 2459's doctrine to ritual, placing those powers on the limbs.

1747 ends: I stood and worshipped Siva's feet within my heart (நின்று தொழுதேன் என் நெஞ்சத்தின் உள்ளே). Verse 3 ends: entering in and meditating, I praise him every day (புக்குநின்று உன்னி யான் போற்றிசெய்வேனே). Both make the place of worship the inside of the worshipper; 1747 adds that the Lord already dwells and moves in the body (உடலின் உடன்கிடந்து).

1748: I brought him in and made my heart his temple (கோயில் என் நெஞ்சம்), I joined the Pure One and I bowed (பணிந்தேன்). 1445: sing, bow (பணிமின்), and when you have bowed he takes the joined heart as his temple (கூடிய நெஞ்சத்துக் கோயிலாய்க் கொள்வனே). 1445 gives as instruction what 1748 reports as done; in 1748 the poet brings the Lord in, in 1445 the Lord takes the heart.

1752 maps Om onto the linga: Om the pedestal, M the neck, U the inner circle, A the linga itself (இலிங்கம் அகாரம்), filled with bindu and nada. Song 1165 maps the five letters onto the Lord's body and adds அகர உகர and Om (அகரவுகர ... ஓம). Both treat the sacred syllables as the parts of the Lord's form.

source_issues: 1749: line 1 carries a stray Latin Y (ஆங்கவை Yமூன்றினும்), flagged as corrupt in the source.
1746: line 2 reads அஞ்கின், probably for அஞ்சின், and தனிச்சுடை ராய், probably for தனிச்சுடராய்.
1741: காற்றிடில் (line 1) may be for கூற்றிடில், and lines 3 and 4 (அத்தரு கோரம் மருடத்துஈ சானனே) are hard to divide and may be corrupt.
1747: தென்தலைக்கு (line 3) is obscure and may be corrupt.
